kurz: The five uses of free cash flow and why the choice between them does more to determine returns than day-to-day operations.

bloecke.md:
Suppose a company earns 10% a year on its equity and retains this profit. A chief executive who holds office there for ten years will, by the end, have personally decided on the use of more than 60% of the capital at work in the business. Over this period, equity grows to around two and a half times its starting value. Everything above the starting value is retained profit whose use someone has decided on. This calculation comes from Buffett. It follows that the central task of top management is capital allocation, that is, deciding where the surplus goes. A good divisional head knows the operating business better.

No one is trained for this task, however. Chief executives come from sales, production, development or administration. Capital allocation is a valuation problem, and valuation questions do not feature in any of these careers.

The number of options is small. Free cash flow can be reinvested in the company's own business. It can also go into acquiring another company, repaying debt, a [[Dividend|dividend]] or buying back the company's own shares. A sixth option is to leave the money where it is. That is also a decision; it is just not spoken out loud. A company whose cash grows over the years is betting that better opportunities will come later.

bloecke.titel: Use of operating cash flow in one year
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a medium-sized industrial group, in € million. Free cash flow after maintenance capital expenditure is €900 million, of which €250 million flows into the company's own business as growth capital expenditure. The remaining €650 million is not enough for acquisitions, distributions and debt repayment, so cash falls by €40 million.

bloecke.md:
## Cost of capital as the benchmark

A use of cash creates value if it earns more than the capital employed costs. When reinvesting in the company's own business, the return on the additional invested capital must therefore be above the cost of capital. The 2025 edition of the KPMG Cost of Capital Study covers around 300 companies, including about two thirds of the DAX 40 constituents. It reports an average [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|WACC]] of 8.5%, with a cost of equity of 9.7% and a levered beta of 1.03. By sector, WACC ranges from 6.3% (energy and raw materials) through 7.0% (real estate) to 9.4% (industrials and technology). The risk-free rate of 2.5% assumed there is now outdated, because ten-year Bunds yielded around 3.5% in mid-September 2026. The cost of capital is therefore probably higher today.

What matters here is the marginal return, that is, the return on newly invested capital, and not the average return. A group can earn 18% [[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]] on its legacy business and still invest every new euro at 6%. The average return conceals this for years, because the profitable legacy business carries the weak new investments along with it. This is why growth programmes often look more convincing in presentations than they are.

bloecke.formel: Marginal return = (NOPAT today − NOPAT 5 years ago) / (Invested capital today − Invested capital 5 years ago)
bloecke.erklaerung: The marginal return is calculated over five years, because individual years are shaped by one-off items, swings in working capital and acquisitions. If the figure is below the cost of capital, any further growth destroys value, even if the average return looks good.
variablen: operating profit after tax and before financing costs, that is, EBIT × (1 − tax rate)
interest-bearing debt plus equity, excluding excess liquidity
bloecke.beispiel: NOPAT rises over five years from €420 million to €510 million, and invested capital from €3,000 million to €4,500 million. Marginal return = 90 / 1,500 = 6.0%. At 510 / 4,500 = 11.3%, the reported ROIC is still above the cost of capital of 8.5%. Because the marginal return is below it, the growth of these five years has nevertheless destroyed value.

bloecke.md:
## Debt repayment

Repaying debt brings a safe return equal to the interest rate saved, after tax. During the zero interest rate period this hardly mattered, but at the borrowing costs of 2026 it carries weight. Against this stands the tax advantage of debt, because interest reduces taxable profit and dividends do not. Corporation tax is 15%, or 15.825% together with the 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it. In addition, there is trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), the level of which depends on the municipal multiplier (Hebesatz). In municipalities with 20,000 or more inhabitants, the multipliers in 2025 were between 250% and 580%. Depending on location, the combined tax burden on a German corporation is therefore around 24.6% to 36.1%, and around 30% to 33% in Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. Interest is fully deductible for corporation tax and solidarity surcharge, but only three quarters of it for trade tax. For trade tax, a quarter of the interest is added back to profit to the extent that an allowance of €200,000 is exceeded (Section 8 no. 1 GewStG (Trade Tax Act)). In the municipalities mentioned, every euro of interest therefore saves around 22 to 31 cents in tax, and around 27 to 29 cents in Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich.

The advantage has limits. The interest barrier (Zinsschranke) under Section 4h EStG (Income Tax Act), which applies to corporations via Section 8a KStG (Corporation Tax Act), only allows net interest expense to be deducted up to 30% of tax EBITDA. If net interest expense is below the exemption threshold (Freigrenze) of three million euros, it does not apply. In addition, the ratios to which loan agreements are linked take no account of the tax advantage. These include net financial debt divided by EBITDA and the interest coverage ratio, that is, [[EBIT]] divided by interest expense. For interest coverage, values below about two are considered critical. This is a rule of thumb from practice; there is no standardised threshold. A company that breaches these limits can no longer decide freely on the other four uses.

## Share buyback

Legally, acquiring own shares requires an authorisation from the [[Annual general meeting (AGM)|annual general meeting]], valid for at most five years (Section 71(1) no. 8 AktG (Stock Corporation Act)). Holdings of own shares may not exceed 10% of the share capital (Section 71(2) AktG). The company has no rights arising from its own shares (Section 71b AktG). Own shares therefore receive no dividend and do not count towards earnings per share, even if they are not formally cancelled under Section 237 AktG. On the balance sheet, they are deducted openly from equity (Section 272(1a) HGB (Commercial Code)) and are therefore not an asset. The safe harbour in Article 5 of the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR), Regulation (EU) No 596/2014, together with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1052, provides that an ongoing programme does not count as market manipulation.

Economically, a [[Share buyback|share buyback]] is a purchase like any other and pays off if the price is below the value. The following illustrative calculation holds everything constant except the buyback price. The company has 100 million shares and annual profit of €300 million (€3.00 per share). The intrinsic value of the equity is €5,000 million including €400 million of cash, that is, €50 per share. All of the cash is used for the buyback.

bloecke.unter: Figures from the table, each as a change from the position before the buyback. Earnings per share rise at every price; intrinsic value per share falls as soon as the buyback price is above the intrinsic value of €50.

bloecke.titel: Effects of a buyback on ratios
bloecke.md:
Earnings per share rise as soon as the company's earnings yield is above the interest earned on the funds used. In the model, they still rise by 7.1% even at a buyback price of €60, while value per share falls by 1.4%. ROE also rises, because equity is openly reduced without anything having changed in the business.

Neither ratio is therefore suitable as proof that a buyback has succeeded. As a target for management board remuneration, however, they are convenient, because a buyback increases them without any operational improvement. The interest forgone on the cash used is not taken into account in the table. At an interest rate of 3.5% and around 30% tax, it reduces earnings per share by about ten cents, but it does not change the effect on value.

Another problem is timing. Buybacks are financed from surplus liquidity, and there is most of it at the end of a long upswing, that is, when share prices are high. In a downturn, when the company's own shares are cheap, programmes are stopped because the balance sheet takes priority. This procyclical pattern has been observed repeatedly. Its magnitude varies with the period and the sample; its direction is stable.

In addition, not every buyback is a distribution. A company that buys back as many shares in a year as it issues through share-based remuneration pays nothing out to its owners. It is merely settling personnel expenses in cash after the fact. The test is simple and needs no model assumption. What counts is the diluted share count over ten years, not the buyback volume in euros. If the share count does not fall, no capital has been returned.

## Growth through acquisitions

A takeover differs from every other use of capital because of the control premium. The buyer pays a price well above the stock market price, and this premium must first be earned through synergies before value is created. Event studies spanning several decades find a stable pattern here. The shareholders of the acquired company gain significantly around the day of the announcement, while the acquirer's shareholders lose slightly or come out at around zero. The frequently quoted failure rates of 70% to 90%, on the other hand, come from consultancy studies with varying definitions of success and are not a measured figure. The widespread claim that “takeovers mostly fail” is therefore not substantiated. What is well founded is the finding that, on average, the gain in value ends up with the seller.

The consequences show up later on the balance sheet. Whatever was paid above the fair value of the net assets acquired appears as [[Goodwill|goodwill]] on the assets side. Under the HGB, it is amortised on a scheduled basis, over ten years if its useful life cannot be reliably estimated (Section 253(3) HGB). Under IFRS, there is no scheduled amortisation, only an impairment test at least once a year under IAS 36. An impairment loss, once recognised, may never be reversed. A company reporting under IFRS can therefore show an overpriced acquisition for years without any visible charge, as long as management sticks to its planning assumptions. For a quick check, deduct goodwill from equity and recalculate the equity ratio.

A company that pays for a takeover with its own shares is selling stakes in its own business. This is the reverse of a buyback. It only pays off for existing shareholders if what is acquired is worth more per share issued than what is given up. If the company's own shares trade below their intrinsic value, a takeover paid for in shares is a losing deal even if the price for the acquired company was fair.

## Executive remuneration and incentives

How a management board allocates capital depends on its incentives. The supervisory board sets a remuneration system for the management board (Section 87a AktG), and the annual general meeting approves it at least every four years (Section 120a AktG). This vote is not directly legally binding, but it is public and comes with an obligation to give reasons. Each year, it is followed by the remuneration report under Section 162 AktG, which the management board and supervisory board prepare jointly and which the auditor reviews formally. Section 87(1) AktG requires the remuneration structure to be geared towards the sustainable and long-term development of the company.

The remuneration report states which ratio the bonus formula is linked to. From this, you can tell which of the five uses the management board is most inclined towards. If the bonus depends on earnings per share, a debt-financed buyback at any price is the most convenient way to reach the target. With revenue, balance sheet total or EBITDA as the target, the company makes acquisitions. A target based on the absolute share price also depends on the performance of the market as a whole, so relative targets against a named peer group are more precise. Only ratios with capital employed in the denominator (ROCE, [[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]], value added relative to the cost of capital) assess growth and return at the same time. Share options work asymmetrically. They produce a gain when prices rise and cost nothing when prices fall, which makes risk and debt attractive. Actual shares locked up with a holding period of several years extending beyond the executive's departure reflect the owners' interests better.

bloecke.unter: At each stage, two figures are compared; strategic preference plays no part. The dividend comes last because it is the only use that is binding in practice. A cut costs more trust than its introduction gained.

schritte.text: Note the diluted share count from the notes to the accounts year by year. It is the most meaningful single figure on capital allocation, because it shows at once whether capital has been returned, whether takeovers were paid for with own shares and what share-based remuneration has cost.

Divide the payments for the acquisition of own shares from the financing cash flow by the number of shares from the statement of changes in equity. Compare the result with today's share price and with your own valuation.

Divide the change in NOPAT over five years by the change in invested capital and compare the result with the industry's cost of capital. If the marginal return is below it, every growth programme needs explaining.
Compare the additions from acquisitions with the later impairments. Many acquisitions with regular write-downs point to excessive purchase prices and not merely to integration problems.
Check in the remuneration report under Section 162 AktG which metric is measured over which period and against which peer group, and whether a buyback or an acquisition can influence it directly.

punkte: Reinvestment only as long as the marginal return is above the cost of capital
Buybacks only below the company's own intrinsic value, and none for years if necessary
Small acquisitions in familiar markets, without paying a premium on an auction price
A dividend that is covered by free cash flow over the long term
Remuneration based on return on capital and relative performance over several years
Growth for its own sake, financed from retained earnings without checking the return
Buybacks at high prices that are halted in a downturn
Large takeovers justified by strategic necessity instead of by a calculation
A dividend maintained despite falling cash flow so as not to break the streak
Bonuses based on earnings per share, revenue or balance sheet total

mitnehmen: If a return on equity of 10% is retained in full, top management decides on more than 60% of the capital at work in the business within ten years. These decisions carry more weight than day-to-day operations.

All five uses are measured against the same hurdle, the cost of capital. For companies from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, it most recently averaged 8.5%, ranging between around 6% and 9.5% depending on the sector.
A buyback only creates value if the price is below intrinsic value. Earnings per share and ROE almost always rise and are therefore no proof of success.

In takeovers, the gain in value ends up with the seller on average. Under IFRS, an excessive price only becomes visible when the goodwill is written down. Under the HGB, goodwill is amortised on a scheduled basis over its expected useful life, and over ten years only if that life cannot be reliably estimated.
The bonus metric in the remuneration report shows more reliably than any strategy presentation where the money will go.

begriffe.text: The decision on how a company uses the surplus it has generated: reinvestment, acquisition, debt repayment, dividend, share buyback or building up cash. All these uses are measured against the same hurdle, the cost of capital.

The change in NOPAT divided by the change in invested capital over several years. It measures what the most recently invested money earns. It can be far below the reported ROIC, because the latter is supported by the legacy business.
The premium over the stock market price that a buyer pays for a majority stake in a company. Synergies must first earn this amount before a takeover creates value for the buyer's shareholders.

Tax restriction on deductions under Section 4h EStG, applied to corporations via Section 8a KStG. Net interest expense is only deductible up to 30% of tax EBITDA, with an exemption threshold of three million euros. The interest barrier thus limits the tax advantage of debt.

Annual report by the management board and supervisory board under Section 162 AktG on the remuneration granted and owed to board members, which the auditor reviews formally. The report names the ratios on which variable remuneration depends.
